source_text: Ἁμαρτάνουσι δὲ οἱ λέγοντες τοῖς προτέροις ἀμείνονα δεδόσθαι βίον, καὶ οὐ συνιᾶσιν, ὅτι πάμπολυ διαφέρει σοφία τῆς τῶν χρημάτων περιουσίας· καὶ τοσοῦτόν ἐστι φανερωτέρα, ὅσον ἄργυρος λαμπρότερος φαίνεται τῆς ἑαυτοῦ σκιᾶς. Ζωὴ γὰρ ἀνθρώπου, οὐκ ἐξ ἐπικήρου πλούτου κτήσεως, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ σοφίας περιγίνεται. Τίς δὲ καὶ δυνήσεται, εἰπέ μοι, τὴν τοσαύτην καὶ οὕτω χρηστὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ πρόνοιαν ἐξειπεῖν; ἢ τίς ἀνακαλέσασθαι τὰ δοκοῦντα παρημελῆσθαι ὑπὸ Θεοῦ δικαίως; Πράττων δὲ οὐκ ὀρθῶς πρότερον ἔγωγε κατενόησα τὰ σύμπαντα, καὶ δίκαιον ἐμμένοντα τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ, καὶ μέχρι θανάτου μὴ ἐξιστάμενον, ἀλλὰ καὶ δι᾽ αὐτὴν ἐπιβουλευόμενον, καὶ ἀσεβῆ συναποθνήσκοντα τῇ ἑαυτοῦ κακίᾳ. Χρὴ δὲ δίκαιον ὄντα μὴ πάνυ τοιοῦτον εἶναι δοκεῖν, μηδὲ ἄγαν σοφὸν καὶ ὑπερμέτρως· ὅπως μή τι πταίσας, πολλαπλασίονα ἁμαρτήσῃ. Καὶ μὴ ἔσο τολμηρὸς καὶ προπετὴς, μή σε θάνατος ἁρπάσῃ ἄκαιρος. Μέγιστον δὲ ἀγαθὸν ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι Θεοῦ, καὶ ἐν τούτῳ ὄντα μηδὲν ἁμαρτάνειν. Τῶν γὰρ ἀμιάντων χειρὶ ἀνάγνῳ ψαύειν, μυσαρόν. Ὁ δὲ μετὰ φόβου Θεοῦ ὑπείκων ἅπαντα διαφεύγει τἀναντία. Σοφία δὲ βοηθείας, στίφους ἀνδρῶν τῶν δυνατωτάτων ἐν πόλει μείζονα δύναται, ἢ καὶ συγγινώσκει δικαίως πολλάκις τῶν δεόντων ἀποτυγχάνουσιν. Ἄπταιστος γάρ ἐστιν οὐδὲ εἷς. Ἀσεβῶν δὲ λόγοις, οὐδ᾽ ὁπωσοῦν τι χρὴ προσιέναι, ὅπως μὴ τῶν κατὰ σοῦ λόγων αὐτήκοος γενόμενος, ὥσπερ δούλου πονηροῦ φλυαρίας· ἔπειτα δηχθεὶς τὴν καρδίαν, ὕστερον ἐν πολλαῖς πράξεσιν εἰς τὸ ἀντικαταράσασθαι καὶ σὺ ἐκτραπῇς.
thought_title: Wisdom outweighs wealth; righteousness without excess
orientation: Wisdom is worth more than wealth, righteousness is not to be pushed beyond measure, and the fear of God keeps a person safe.
pass_a_gloss: They err who say a better life was given to the former ones, and do not understand that wisdom differs very much from abundance of money; and is so much more manifest as silver appears brighter than its own shadow. For man's life results not from acquisition of perishable wealth, but from wisdom. Who will be able, tell me, to declare so great and so kind providence of God? Or who to call back the things seeming to have been neglected by God justly? Doing not rightly formerly, I observed all things: both a just man abiding in justice and not departing until death, but even plotted against through it, and an ungodly man dying together with his own wickedness. One being just must not seem to be very much such, nor too wise and beyond measure, lest stumbling in something you sin manifold. And do not be bold and rash, lest untimely death snatch you. Greatest good to lay hold of God, and being in this to sin in nothing. For to touch the undefiled with impure hand is abominable. He who yields with fear of God escapes all contrary things. Wisdom is capable of greater help than a band of the most powerful men in a city, which also justly pardons often those failing of what is due. For no one is unstumbling. To words of the ungodly one must not in any way give heed, lest becoming an ear-witness of words against you, like the babble of a wicked slave, then stung in heart, later in many doings you too turn aside to cursing in return.

pass_b_english: Those who say that a better life was granted to the people of former times are mistaken (Ecclesiastes 7:10). They do not understand that wisdom far surpasses an abundance of money, and is as much more conspicuous as silver shines brighter than its own shadow (Ecclesiastes 7:11-12). For a person's life comes not from acquiring perishable wealth but from wisdom (Ecclesiastes 7:12). Tell me, who will be able to describe in full the providence of God, so great and so kind? Or who will call back what God seems, and justly, to have left neglected (Ecclesiastes 7:13)? In earlier days, when I did not act rightly, I observed all things: a righteous man holding fast to righteousness and not turning from it even until death, and even plotted against because of it; and an ungodly man dying together with his own wickedness (Ecclesiastes 7:15).

If you are righteous, you should not appear exceedingly so, nor too wise, beyond measure, lest you stumble somewhere and sin many times over (Ecclesiastes 7:16). Do not be bold and rash, lest an untimely death snatch you away (Ecclesiastes 7:17). The greatest good is to lay hold of God and, remaining in this, to commit no sin. For to touch what is undefiled with an unclean hand is an abomination. He who submits with the fear of God escapes every adversity (Ecclesiastes 7:18). Wisdom can give greater help than a band of the mightiest men in a city (Ecclesiastes 7:19), and it often justly pardons those who fall short of what they ought to do; for there is not one who never stumbles (Ecclesiastes 7:20). Give the words of the ungodly no hearing at all, so that you do not hear with your own ears what is said against you, like the chatter of a wicked slave, and then, stung to the heart, you too later turn aside in many of your dealings to curse in return (Ecclesiastes 7:21-22).
notes: Numbering is the same in English and LXX. Gregory gives no clear paraphrase of 7:14, so it is not cited. 'Who will call back what God seems, and justly, to have left neglected?' takes δικαίως with παρημελῆσθαι; it could also go with ἀνακαλέσασθαι ('rightly call back'). It reworks LXX 7:13 'who can set straight what God has made crooked?'. 'When I did not act rightly' renders πράττων οὐκ ὀρθῶς πρότερον, Gregory's form of 'in the days of my vanity' (7:15); it could also mean 'when I fared badly'. 'Remaining in this' renders ἐν τούτῳ ὄντα; the pronoun may also mean 'in him' (God). 'To touch what is undefiled with an unclean hand' freely echoes LXX 7:18 'do not defile your hand'; it is cited with the verse as a whole. Doubtful reading: the copy-text prints ἢ καὶ συγγινώσκει; the English follows ἣ ('and it ... pardons', wisdom as subject), as the 1622 Latin relative 'Quae etiam ... iuste ignoscit' implies; the 1622 Greek glyph is too worn to decide (see source row note). The command against heeding the ungodly is impersonal in Greek (χρή) but turns to 'you'; the English uses the second person throughout.
